6. Mr. Salahuddin, learned Advocate appearing ter the plaintiff, on the other hand submits that irrespective of the arbitration award obtained in London and a decree from the High Court of Justice, Queens Bench Division, England in pursuance of the award, a fresh suit for recovery of money on the basis of charter-party is legally maintainable since the defendant has no property in England to satisfy I he award. The learned Advocate further submits that though Bangladesh is a signatory of the New York Convention on the recognition and enforcement of foreign Arbitral Award a foreign arbitration award in not executable in view of explanation 3 to Section 44A C.P.C. and as such, a civil suit is legally maintainable. 

 13. The defendant, in fact, filed the application under section 151 for rejection of the plaint. The application was made on the ground that the plaintiff seeks to enforce the award of the arbitrators and the decree of the High Court of Justice, Queens Bench Division, England which cannot be executed in Bangladesh in view of clause (b) of Explanation 3 of Section 44A of the Code which clearly excludes a foreign arbitration award or a decree, that the court does not have jurisdiction to entertain the suit and that there is no enactment in Bangladesh providing legal mechanism tor enforcement of foreign arbitral award or judgment. This, seems to us that the submission of the learned Advocate is opposite to the points agitated before the learned Subordinate Judge. The learned Subordinate Judge repelled the contentions holding that the plaintiff instituted the suit independent of the arbitration award on payment of advorem court fee for realization of money on a fresh cause of action and that in the plaint, the plaintiff made averments regarding the arbitration proceeding only to show the circumstances for which the plaintiff is compelled to institute the suit. We arc in respectful agreement with the learned Subordinate Judge that the suit is instituted on a fresh cause of action which is legally maintainable. 

 15. The decision in the case of Burmah Eastern Ltd. was considered by our Appellate Division in the case of Guiness Peat (Trading) Limited Vs. Md. Fazlur Rahman, 44 DLR (AD) 242. That was also a money suit instituted against a trading company of London for supply of goods of inferior quality, the plaintiff rejected the goods but for mitigating his loss, sold the goods and instituted the suit. The defendant filed an application for rejection of the plaint on the ground that the court had no jurisdiction to adjudicate upon the suit since the defendant does not reside or carry on business in Bangladesh and that no cause of action arose within the jurisdiction of the court of Bangladesh. In that case, it was argued that if the suit is allowed to proceed it would be contrary to the principles of private international law and that any decree that may be made in the suit would not be binding on the foreign defendant. Their Lordships repelled the contentions holding inter alia: 

 "44A (I) where a certified copy of a decree of any of the superior courts of the United Kingdom or any reciprocating territory has been filed in a District Court, the decree may be executed in Bangladesh as if it had been passed by the District Court  (2)   (3) 

 Explanation 3 "Decree" with reference to a Superior Court, means any decree or judgment of such court under which a sum of money is payable, not being a sum payable in respect of taxes or other charges of a like nature or in respect of a tine or other penalty, and (a) (b) in no case includes an arbitration award, even if such award is enforceable as a decree or judgment." 

 Section 44A of the Code provides that a decree of superior courts of United Kingdom or a reciprocating country can be executed in Bangladesh as if it had been passed by the District Court i.e. the local limits of the jurisdiction of a principal Civil Court of original jurisdiction. If such decree falls within the exceptions specified in Section 13 of the Code, the District Court shall refuse execution of such decree. Decree with reference to a "Superior Court" does not include an arbitration award even if such award is enforceable as a decree as per clause (b) of Explanation 3 of Section 44A. Therefore the arbitration award given by the arbitrators and the decree passed by the High Court of Justice, Queens Bench, in pursuance of the award cannot be executed in Bangladesh Similar point was raised before the Appellate Division in the case of Bangladesh Air Service (PVT) Vs. British Airways PLC, 49 DLR (AD) 187, their Lordships though found the point not very much relevant for the disposal of the case, but .answered the point succinctly: 

 We fully agree with the views expressed by the Supreme Court of India. If statutory enactments are clear in meaning, they must be construed according to their meaning even though they are contrary to Inter-national Law. We have, therefore, no hesitation in corning to the conclusion that a foreign arbitration award even if such award is enforceable as a decree or judgment of the United Kingdom cannot be executed in Bangladesh in view of clause (b), explanation-3 of Section 44A of the Code of Civil Procedure even if Bangladesh is a signatory of the New York Convention 1958 on the recognition and enforcement of foreign arbitral award. Therefore, we do not find any substance in the submission of the learned Advocate for the defendant-petit toner. 

 19. As regards the points agitated before the learned Subordinate Judge that the plaintiff is in fact enforcing the award indirectly in the form of a suit is also merits no consideration. From the averments made in the plaint, we find that the plaintiff did not seek to enforce the award and the decree in the disguise of a suit.
